reading.body:
Six of the eight MCP clients listed here are coding tools, and five are open-source, which together signal that MCP adoption is currently concentrated in software development workflows rather than spread across general-purpose AI applications.

The protocol's first client family came from Anthropic, the same organization that created MCP. The rest of the field is made up of independent coding agents and editors, including contributions from Microsoft and Block. That distribution suggests the protocol spread quickly through developer tooling communities, where connecting AI assistants to local context and external services has immediate practical value.

This data covers clients only, not servers, so it says nothing about what those clients are actually connecting to or how heavily any of them are used. It does not touch compute, infrastructure, or power consumption, because MCP is a coordination protocol, not a compute layer. The pattern here is about software interoperability standards, and it stands at a distance from the grid and buildings arguments that govern AI scaling at larger scope.
